title: Bad breath
hook: angry at someone's bad breath? what can he do, it's his mouth (Meditations 5.28)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Heraclitus. Your line was the river. What did you let move past today, a worry or a win? Day five hundred seventy.

Of all the things you might expect in the private notebook of a Roman emperor, a note about body odor is near the bottom of the list. And yet there it is, in the twenty-eighth entry of book five. He doesn't say whether he had anyone in mind. But the picture he sketches is vivid: sweaty armpits, bad breath, and someone close enough to notice, getting irritated. He uses it to think something through, and it's very practical. Today: bad breath.
screen: `AN EMPEROR'S NOTEBOOK.` → `A NOTE ABOUT BODY ODOR.` → `BAD BREATH.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Are you angry with someone whose armpits smell? Marcus asks himself. Angry with someone whose breath is bad? What good will that do you? Second, the plain answer. He has the mouth he has, Marcus says, and the armpits he has. A smell like that has to come from things like that. That's the whole carry: it's his mouth. A lot of small annoyances work the same way. The loud chewer. The slow walker. The coworker who says actually before every sentence. These come out of who they are and how they're made, not out of a plan to bother you. Third, but he has reason. Then Marcus imagines an objection. But the man has reason, you'll say; he could notice and fix it. Fine, Marcus replies. You have reason too. So use your reasoning to stir up his. Show him. Tell him, kindly. If he listens, you'll have cured it, and there's no need for anger. Fourth, no drama. And Marcus finishes by saying there's no need for theatrics either. Not the tragic actor, he says, and not the opposite extreme. Just calm, plain dealing. Here's why this tiny entry matters. It breaks every small annoyance into two honest options. Either it's not theirs to change, in which case anger is pointless. Or it is, in which case a kind word works better than anger does. Either way, anger isn't needed. And there's something warm under the joke: Marcus's answer is not to avoid the man, but to help him.
screen: `ANGRY AT BAD BREATH? WHAT GOOD IS IT?` · `HE HAS THE MOUTH HE HAS.` · `YOU HAVE REASON TOO: TELL HIM KINDLY.` · `NO NEED FOR THEATRICS.` · then, large: `IT'S HIS MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small annoyance from someone you see often: a habit, a sound, a way of talking. Notice whether there's a little spark of irritation. Then ask Marcus's two questions. Is this something they can change? If not, say quietly: it's his mouth, or her mouth, and let it go. If they can, picture telling them, kindly, once. Either way, see whether the anger has anything left to do. The bell holds the time.
Bad breath. Marcus asks what good anger does at someone's smell: he has the mouth he has. If it can be fixed, tell him kindly. Today's word.
Your line: it's his mouth. Forgive one small annoyance today, or, if it can be changed, mention it once, kindly, without anger. Day five hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes recall Meditations 5.28 with small irritations: either it can't be helped, so let it go, or it can, so mention it kindly.

notes: 5.28 paraphrased: are you angry with him whose armpits stink, or whose mouth smells foul? What good will this anger do? He has such a mouth, such armpits; such an emanation must come from such things. But the man has reason, it will be said; he could perceive his offense. Well, you have reason too: stir up his rational faculty by yours, show him, admonish him; if he listens, you will cure him, and there is no need of anger. The closing phrase (neither tragic actor nor harlot) is softened to 'no need for theatrics... not the opposite extreme'. Confirm.
Marcus names no one; the hook says so. Whether the entry reflects a real person or is a general example is unknown.
The trapdoor's 'classic Stoic move' is interpretive; confirm or soften.

Editor review (year 2, days 558–575): the hook invented Marcus 'standing close, getting irritated' (5.28 names no scene) and called it 'one of the most practical entries'; both cut. Sweeping 'most of what annoys us' softened; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel; trapdoor's 'classic Stoic move' made textual.
